title: Distributed Email Service
oneLine: Separate SMTP ingress/egress from mailbox metadata, object attachments, search, and realtime sync; make delivery retryable while protecting reputation and abuse boundaries.
opening: I would split mail transport from mailbox serving. Inbound SMTP gateways validate the envelope, apply connection/reputation controls, scan spam and malware, persist the raw MIME message durably, then enqueue mailbox delivery. Metadata—folder, thread, sender, recipients, flags, timestamps—is sharded primarily by user ID; large bodies and attachments stay in object storage. A search pipeline builds a per-user index. Web/mobile clients use HTTPS for mailbox APIs and push hints for new mail, but synchronize from a durable change cursor. Outbound mail is accepted into a durable queue, authenticated and scanned, then sent through warmed IP/domain pools with retry rules based on SMTP status. Bounces and feedback loops update reputation and delivery status. Transactional and bulk traffic are isolated so abuse or a campaign cannot damage critical mail.
ask: Consumer mailbox, transactional sender, or both?
Retention, compliance, encryption, and data locality?
Delivery latency, volume, and anti-spam/reputation requirements?
scale: Mailbox metadata and search operations may dominate request QPS; attachment bytes dominate storage/egress.
Shard by user so mailbox list/update operations stay local; a message addressed to many users creates per-mailbox references.
SMTP retries may last hours/days, so queue/storage and status lifecycle must support long delays.

decisions.default: Metadata in sharded database, raw body/attachments in durable object storage, search in derived index.
decisions.why: Each workload has different access and scaling characteristics.
decisions.switch: Small systems can store body in a relational/blob store first, but preserve clear boundaries.

decisions.why: Most reads, flags, folders, and sync are per user and require consistency.
decisions.switch: Large enterprise tenants may receive dedicated shards and secondary partitions.

decisions.default: Use message headers plus normalized subject/participants heuristics, stored as derived thread metadata.
decisions.why: Internet mail lacks one globally reliable thread ID.
decisions.switch: Internal-only mail can use a controlled conversation ID.

decisions.default: Push notification as hint, durable per-user change log/cursor as truth.
decisions.why: Devices can be offline and push is lossy.
decisions.switch: IMAP compatibility can be layered over the same mailbox state with protocol-specific sequence semantics.

deepDives.title: Deliverability
points: Separate transactional, marketing, and untrusted tenant IP/domain pools.
Warm new IPs gradually; sign with DKIM, publish SPF/DMARC, process complaints/bounces quickly.
Throttle by destination domain and adapt to transient 4xx responses.

deepDives.title: Mailbox mutations
points: Flags/folder moves are idempotent and versioned per user.
A durable change sequence supports device sync and conflict resolution.
Read/unread counters are derived and periodically reconciled.

deepDives.title: Security
points: Sandbox MIME parsers and attachment scanners; never trust content type or filenames.
Encrypt in transit/at rest and use scoped object URLs.
Protect account recovery, forwarding rules, and OAuth tokens as high-risk controls.

failures.response: Classify 4xx as retry with exponential schedule and domain throttling; 5xx becomes permanent bounce.
Use SMTP/message delivery IDs and idempotent mailbox insertion; preserve legitimate same-Message-ID edge cases carefully.
Mailbox store remains source of truth; rebuild per-user index from raw/metadata and expose freshness.
Tenant quotas, behavior detection, isolated sending pools, rapid suspension, and feedback-loop processing.

questions.q: How do you shard a message sent to 100K recipients?
questions.a: Store raw MIME/content once, then fan out lightweight mailbox references/metadata by recipient shard. Delivery is asynchronous and idempotent; large-list sending also needs consent and rate controls.
An asynchronous per-user inverted index over authorized mailbox content. Query always scopes by user/tenant, and deletion/retention events remove indexed documents with reconciliation.

questions.q: Why is SMTP delivery not exactly once?
questions.a: Timeouts can occur after the remote server accepted the message, so retry may duplicate. Use stable IDs and recipient-side dedupe where possible, but Internet SMTP fundamentally has uncertainty.

questions.q: How do clients sync after being offline?
questions.a: They present the last mailbox change cursor, receive ordered deltas or a reset snapshot if expired, then advance the cursor. Push only signals that a delta exists.

mistakes: One database table for metadata, bodies, attachments, and search
Treating SMTP timeout as definite failure
Using push as authoritative mailbox sync
seniorSignal: Balance protocol uncertainty, mailbox consistency, storage/search separation, reputation economics, and hostile-content isolation. Delivery status must be semantically honest.
implementation: Postfix/SMTP edge concepts with durable Kafka queues
Cassandra/relational mailbox metadata sharded by user
Elasticsearch/OpenSearch per-tenant index; WebSocket push plus cursor API
